column1: # Hmong numeral classifiers and quantifiers, for addition to the ontology.
# TWO SOURCES, both read from their own description rather than from a wordlist.
# White is the base analysis and Bisang fleshes it out: White's is the later and
# fuller treatment, it covers Green Mong as well as White Hmong, and it states its
# disagreements with Bisang explicitly, so it is the one whose categories this file
# follows. Bisang then supplies what White leaves out -- measure words, class
# nouns, the finer [+-exact]/[+-entity] distinctions -- and the forms White's
#   W:<page>  White, Nathan M. 2021. The Hmong language of North Queensland.
#             PhD thesis, James Cook University. DOI 10.25903/f5rd-s089.
#             classifiers-white2021.tsv, whose own header records its
#             uncertainties; this file is the merge.
#   B:<page>  Bisang, Walter. 1993. Classifiers, quantifiers and class nouns in
#             Hmong. Studies in Language 17(1): 1-51. Appendix I is the
#             classifier and quantifier inventory (pp. 31-41), Appendix II the
#             class nouns (pp. 42-45). Use the 51-page published article: the
#   L         this repository's stopwords_classifiers.txt, which gives a form
#             and a class but no definition. It turns out to be an index into
#             White's chapter 7: its headings "locational classifiers" and
#             "verb classifiers" are his categories, and Bisang has no
# CLASS follows the five-way taxonomy of Bond and Paik (2000), as used by
# Morgado da Costa and Bond (2016) when adding classifiers to wordnet:
#   sortal     classify the kind of the noun phrase they quantify
#   mensural   measure an amount of some property
#   group      refer to a collection of members
# WHITE_CATEGORY and BISANG_CATEGORY record the two sources' own analyses, in that
# order, so that the mapping onto Bond and Paik stays inspectable and reversible in
# both directions. Either may be empty: the source in question does not treat that
#   White's own subclasses, which CLASS follows where they are given:
#   Bisang, where White has no category for the form, follows T'sou (1976) on the
# WHAT BISANG ADDS TO WHITE, AND WHERE THEY DISAGREE. The NOTE column flags every
# form whose class differs between them. Taking White as the base, Bisang's
# contribution is of three kinds, and the first two are the reason this file is a
# merge rather than a copy of chapter 7:
#   1. Measure words, which White excludes and Bisang counts. White (p. 366)
#      states they are "not part of the system of noun categorization"; Bisang's
#      Appendix I section 2.1 treats them as measures, which is why this file has
#      ntiv, mev, lav, dos, tshim, xib, taus and the rest. Ten such rows are
#      flagged in NOTE. This is the single biggest addition Bisang makes, and the
#      single biggest difference between the two inventories.
#   2. Class nouns, which White rejects outright -- see item 5 below.
#   3. Finer categories inside White's mensural class. White collapses measures,
#      intrinsic quantifiers, collectives and kinds into one mensural category
#      (pp. 301-302); Bisang keeps them as separate categories, the intrinsic
#      quantifiers being a middle region where the measuring norm comes from the
#      quantified object's own shape rather than from outside it. White's collapse
#      is a deliberate revision of Bisang, not an oversight, so CLASS follows
#      White and BISANG_CATEGORY preserves the finer distinction.
#   4. Where White has a category and Bisang has none, the row rests on White
#      alone: this is all of his locational and verbal action classifiers (his
#      7.3 and 7.6.2), for which Bisang has no category at all.
#   5. Class nouns. White rejects Bisang's class-noun analysis of phau, lo and
#      the rest outright: Bisang "does not provide evidence that would support
#      this class noun analysis" (p. 359), it "would obscure otherwise clear
#      ordering test does not hold up (pp. 359-361). Since class_nouns.tsv is
#      built on Bisang's Appendix II, this is a live disagreement about the
#      whole file and not merely about a category label.
#   6. cov. Four analyses of one form. Bisang calls it the plural marker (p. 8).
#      White makes it a classifier: "Hmong has two non-singular classifiers: cov
#      'CL:PA' and tej 'CL:SOME'" (p. 354), polyfunctional between classifier and
#      external/) argues it is a plural classifier generating a cover, a set of
#      sets. The stopword list files it as mensural, agreeing with none of them.
#      The CLASS given here follows White; the NOTE records the rest.
#   7. The taxonomic class rests on contested ground. Its three rows are Bisang's
#      Class IV, hom and yam. An undated 2016 working note in external/ reports
#      that Heimbach and Mottin list these as classifiers while Jay Xiong and
#      Yuepheng Xiong call them nouns, and is itself undecided: yam usually
#      appears with no noun to classify, and in frames like ib yam li it behaves
#      more like an adverb. Kept as taxonomic because both Bisang and White treat
#      it as a category, but a reader should know the word class is disputed.
#   8. Tone-melody alternation. White (Sec. 2.3.1) shows that daig, riag,
#      nploog, ntsug, ce and tug are alternants of daim, riam, nplooj, ntsuj,
#      cev and tus, not separate classifiers. The stopword list lists them as if
#      they were. Flagged in NOTE; kept as rows so the alternation is recorded.
# WHAT WHITE'S SECTION 1.5.2.1 DOES AND DOES NOT DO. It is a descriptive precis
# of Bisang (pp. 25-27) -- the four operations, the [+-exact]/[+-entity]
# parameters, the five-way split, the Noun > Class Noun > Quantifier > Intrinsic
# Quantifier > Classifier cline -- and passes no judgement. His verdict is in
# FUNCTION records Bisang's classifier / quantifier / class noun distinction,
# which White does not draw: it is one of the things Bisang adds.
# Several forms do more than one job: he shows zaj and qhov doing two or three at
# DIALECT: WH = White Hmong (Hmoob Dawb, mww), GM = Green Mong (Hmoob Ntsuab,
# hnj) -- the tags this repository and White both use. White covers both varieties,
# which is a second reason to take him as the base; Bisang describes White Hmong
# throughout (p. 45 n. 1), so every Green Mong row rests on White. Where White
# gives one form for both varieties it appears here as two rows, one per dialect.
# DEFINITION follows the template of Morgado da Costa and Bond (2016):
# "a ... classifier used ...". Rows with an empty DEFINITION are attested in the
# stopword list and described by neither source; they are deliberately left for
# EXAMPLES are Hmong noun + English gloss pairs taken from the source, with the
# classifier stripped, so lub thoob 'bucket' appears as thoob (bucket). They are
# what the converter turns into `classifies` relations. For verbal_action rows
# the items are the co-occurring verbs, not nouns.
# NOTE carries per-row disagreements and caveats. Empty means neither source
# DISPOSITION says what the converter should do with a row that is not a plain
# classifier. Empty means add it normally.
#   variant-of:<form>  the row is a tone-melody alternant of <form> (White,
#                      so it becomes a <variant> of that lemma rather than a lemma
#                      of its own. Six rows: daig of daim, riag of riam, nploog of
#                      nplooj, ntsug of ntsuj, ce of cev, and tug of tus. The last
#                      needs care: tug is ALSO the Green Mong cognate of tus, and
#                      that row stands separately as a Green Mong lemma, so the
#                      form alone does not identify the dialect.
#                      ce attaches to the ontology's existing noun cev 'body',
#                      not to a classifier, because cev is not a classifier.
#   omit               the stopword list has the form but no source supports it as
#                      a classifier, so it is not added. Six rows: txog and txug
#                      (only the verb 'arrive'), cev (only the noun 'body'), dlus
#                      (a measure word, which White excludes from the classifier
#                      system), npaug (glossed CL:TIMES only in an appendix text,
#                      p. 675, not in chapter 7), and khaw (White has khawv
#                      'CL:BITE' at p. 337, a form occurring once and never
#                      discussed, so its tone-bearing final could not be checked).
#                      The rows are kept rather than deleted so the evidence for
#                      omitting them is on the record.
#                      CHECK: Nathan -- especially cev, and whether khaw/khawv is
